newsitem.title: USA: FCC's Hundt wants new laws to spur phone competition.
newsitem.headline: FCC's Hundt wants new laws to spur phone competition.

text.p: Saying last year's sweeping communications law is not working, the nation's top telephone regulator Thursday said new laws are needed to open the $100 billion local phone market because it remains closed to competition.

Outgoing Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt urged Congress to give his agency more power to interpret the act and punish violators of FCC rules -- 18 months after the landmark law was signed by President Clinton.

He also said lawmakers should consolidate court challenges of FCC rules in one court. Hundt said fights the FCC must wage in courts nationwide are slowing the entry of long-distance carriers and others into the local phone business.
"By no means am I saying the whole thing needs to be reopened," Hundt said of the law in an interview. "Just clear up the weed patch of the legal process."

Lamakers, long-distance companies such as AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp., and others complain that the 1996 law so far has failed to open the local phone market controlled by the regional Baby Bells and GTE Corp.

A U.S. appeals court in St. Louis recently threw out key FCC rules aimed at doing just that -- saying the agency had overstepped its authority and taken away key powers that should be in the hands of state regulators.

"We have a major challenge to introduce competition into local telephone markets. And that challenge is not being met," Hundt said earlier in a speech to the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank.
Among other recommendations to Congress, Hundt called for legislation that would:
-- Combine legal challenges to FCC rules into one case that would be heard by a single court. The court would face deadlines to issue rulings.
-- Give the FCC national enforcement powers so it can impose stiffer penalties on companies that violate FCC regulations implementing the law.
-- Make it tougher for courts to strike down FCC rules by ensuring that judges give the agency's regulations "deference" when hearing challenges. Hundt cited legal precedents for such a move.
-- Allow the agency to spell out key terms in the law, such as the word "cost" associated with operating a local phone network. That would make it tougher for FCC rules to become ensnared in court.
